Least squares, the Gaussian likelihood, nonconvex optimization, collinearity, data preparation, and selection bias.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.linalg import qr, solve_triangular
from scipy.optimize import minimize

np.set_printoptions(precision=6, suppress=True)
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)

Question 1 (Least squares and matrix calculations)

Set the random seed to 43201. Generate n=100n = 100 observations with p=5p = 5 predictors,

xij∼iidN(0,1),εi∼iidN(0,0.72),x_{ij} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1), \qquad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, 0.7^2),

with 𝑿=[𝟏𝒙1⋯𝒙5]\mathbf X = [\mathbf 1 \ \ \mathbf x_1 \ \cdots \ \mathbf x_5], 𝜷=(3,1.4,−0.9,0.7,0,1.1)𝖳\boldsymbol\beta = (3, 1.4, -0.9, 0.7, 0, 1.1)^{\mathsf T}, and 𝒚=𝑿𝜷+𝜺\mathbf y = \mathbf X \boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon.

(a) Generate the data; report the dimensions and rank of 𝑿\mathbf X; compute 𝜷̂\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}

rng = np.random.default_rng(43201)

n, p = 100, 5
sigma_true = 0.7

X_pred = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, size=(n, p))          # the five predictors
eps    = rng.normal(0.0, sigma_true, size=n)        # the errors

X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), X_pred])           # add the intercept column
beta_true = np.array([3.0, 1.4, -0.9, 0.7, 0.0, 1.1])
y = X @ beta_true + eps

print("dim(X) =", X.shape)
print("rank(X) =", np.linalg.matrix_rank(X), " (full column rank:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(X) == X.shape[1], ")")
dim(X) = (100, 6)
rank(X) = 6  (full column rank: True )

np.linalg.lstsq solves the least-squares problem through an SVD-based driver, so 𝜷̂\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} is obtained without ever forming 𝑿𝖳𝑿\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X or inverting it. Standard errors below are computed from the 𝑹\mathbf R factor of a QR decomposition (again no explicit inverse of 𝑿𝖳𝑿\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X).

beta_hat, _, rank_ls, sing_vals = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)

# standard errors via the QR factor: (X'X)^{-1} = R^{-1} R^{-T}
Q, R = qr(X, mode="economic")
Rinv = solve_triangular(R, np.eye(R.shape[0]))
xtx_inv_diag = np.sum(Rinv**2, axis=1)

resid_tmp = y - X @ beta_hat
sigma2_unbiased = resid_tmp @ resid_tmp / (n - X.shape[1])
se = np.sqrt(sigma2_unbiased * xtx_inv_diag)

coef_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "true beta": beta_true,
    "beta hat": beta_hat,
    "difference": beta_hat - beta_true,
    "std. error": se,
    "diff / SE": (beta_hat - beta_true) / se,
}, index=["intercept", "x1", "x2", "x3", "x4", "x5"])

print("rank reported by lstsq:", rank_ls)
coef_table.round(4)
rank reported by lstsq: 6
true beta beta hat difference std. error diff / SE
intercept 3.0 2.9731 -0.0269 0.0689 -0.3908
x1 1.4 1.3240 -0.0760 0.0722 -1.0520
x2 -0.9 -0.8415 0.0585 0.0589 0.9931
x3 0.7 0.7204 0.0204 0.0687 0.2976
x4 0.0 -0.0831 -0.0831 0.0646 -1.2873
x5 1.1 1.1651 0.0651 0.0646 1.0069

Comparison. 𝑿\mathbf X is 100×6100 \times 6 and has rank 6, so it is of full column rank and the least-squares solution is unique. Every estimate lands close to the coefficient that generated the data: the largest discrepancy is 0.0830.083, on β4\beta_4, whose true value is 00. Dividing each difference by its standard error, all six estimates sit within about 1.31.3 standard errors of the truth, which is exactly what sampling variation at n=100n = 100 and σ=0.7\sigma = 0.7 should produce. In particular the estimate of the null coefficient β4=0\beta_4 = 0 is not exactly zero — least squares has no mechanism to return an exact zero — but it is statistically indistinguishable from zero.

(b) Fitted values, residuals, and training RMSE

fitted = X @ beta_hat
r = y - fitted
rss = r @ r
rmse_train = np.sqrt(np.mean(r**2))

print(f"RSS               = {rss:.6f}")
print(f"training RMSE     = {rmse_train:.6f}")
print(f"true sigma        = {sigma_true:.6f}")
print(f"mean of residuals = {r.mean():.3e}")
print("\nfirst 5 observations:")
pd.DataFrame({"y": y[:5], "fitted": fitted[:5], "residual": r[:5]}).round(4)

The training RMSE is 0.64630.6463, slightly below the true noise level σ=0.7\sigma = 0.7. That is expected: the training RMSE divides by nn rather than n−p−1n - p - 1, and the fitted coefficients were chosen to minimize exactly this quantity on this sample, so it is an optimistically small estimate of the noise scale.

(c) ‖𝑿𝖳𝒓‖∞\lVert \mathbf X^{\mathsf T} \mathbf r \rVert_\infty

grad_norm = np.max(np.abs(X.T @ r))
print(f"||X' r||_inf = {grad_norm:.3e}")
print(f"scale for comparison, ||X' y||_inf = {np.max(np.abs(X.T @ y)):.3f}")
||X' r||_inf = 1.479e-12
scale for comparison, ||X' y||_inf = 305.210

Why this is essentially zero. The least-squares criterion S(𝜷)=‖𝒚−𝑿𝜷‖2S(\boldsymbol\beta) = \lVert \mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\rVert^2 has gradient −2𝑿𝖳(𝒚−𝑿𝜷)-2\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta). Setting it to zero gives the normal equations 𝑿𝖳(𝒚−𝑿𝜷̂)=𝑿𝖳𝒓=𝟎\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}) = \mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf r = \mathbf 0, so the exact minimizer makes this vector identically zero. The computed value, on the order of 10−1210^{-12}, is pure floating-point rounding: it is roughly machine epsilon relative to the scale of 𝑿𝖳𝒚\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y, which confirms the solver returned an accurate solution.

What it says about 𝒓\mathbf r. The residual vector is orthogonal to every column of 𝑿\mathbf X. Geometrically, 𝒚̂\widehat{\mathbf y} is the orthogonal projection of 𝒚\mathbf y onto the column space of 𝑿\mathbf X and 𝒓\mathbf r lies in the orthogonal complement. Two immediate consequences: because the first column is 𝟏\mathbf 1, the residuals sum to zero (shown above as a mean of order 10−1610^{-16}), and because each 𝒙j\mathbf x_j is a column, the residuals are uncorrelated with every predictor — there is no remaining linear signal in 𝑿\mathbf X for the model to extract.

Question 2 (Gaussian likelihood for linear regression)

With 𝒀∣𝑿∼Nn(𝑿𝜷,σ2𝑰n)\mathbf Y \mid \mathbf X \sim N_n(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2 \mathbf I_n),

ℓ(𝜷,σ2)=−n2log⁡(2πσ2)−12σ2(𝒚−𝑿𝜷)𝖳(𝒚−𝑿𝜷).\ell(\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta).

(a) For fixed σ2\sigma^2, maximizing ℓ\ell over 𝜷\boldsymbol\beta is minimizing the RSS

Write RSS(𝜷)=(𝒚−𝑿𝜷)𝖳(𝒚−𝑿𝜷)\mathrm{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta) = (\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta)^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta). Then

ℓ(𝜷,σ2)=−n2log⁡(2πσ2)⏟free of 𝜷−12σ2RSS(𝜷).\ell(\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2) = \underbrace{-\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)}_{\text{free of } \boldsymbol\beta} \;-\; \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\,\mathrm{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta).

For fixed σ2\sigma^2 the first term is a constant in 𝜷\boldsymbol\beta, and the second is RSS(𝜷)\mathrm{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta) multiplied by the strictly negative constant −1/(2σ2)-1/(2\sigma^2). A strictly decreasing affine transformation reverses the ordering of a function’s values, so 𝜷\boldsymbol\beta maximizes ℓ\ell if and only if it minimizes RSS(𝜷)\mathrm{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta) — and the argmax does not depend on the value of σ2\sigma^2.

Implication. Under the Gaussian model with i.i.d. homoscedastic errors, the maximum-likelihood estimate of 𝜷\boldsymbol\beta is the least-squares estimate: 𝜷̂MLE=𝜷̂OLS=𝜷̂\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{OLS}} = \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}, which here is unique because 𝑿\mathbf X has full column rank. Least squares, normally motivated as a geometric projection, is thus given a probabilistic justification; the equivalence is a consequence of Gaussian errors with constant variance and would fail for other error distributions.

(b) MLE of σ2\sigma^2 for fixed 𝜷\boldsymbol\beta

Treat v=σ2v = \sigma^2 as the argument and differentiate:

ℓ(𝜷,v)=−n2log⁡(2π)−n2log⁡v−RSS(𝜷)2v,∂ℓ∂v=−n2v+RSS(𝜷)2v2.\ell(\boldsymbol\beta, v) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\log v - \frac{\mathrm{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)}{2v}, \qquad \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial v} = -\frac{n}{2v} + \frac{\mathrm{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)}{2v^{2}}.

Setting the derivative to zero and multiplying by 2v2>02v^2 > 0 gives −nv+RSS(𝜷)=0-nv + \mathrm{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta) = 0, so

σ̂MLE2=RSS(𝜷)n.\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \frac{\mathrm{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)}{n}.

This is a maximum: ∂ℓ/∂v>0\partial\ell/\partial v > 0 for v<RSS/nv < \mathrm{RSS}/n and <0< 0 for v>RSS/nv > \mathrm{RSS}/n, so ℓ\ell increases then decreases. Equivalently ∂2ℓ/∂v2=n/(2v2)−RSS/v3\partial^2\ell/\partial v^2 = n/(2v^2) - \mathrm{RSS}/v^3, which equals −n3/(2RSS2)<0-n^3/(2\,\mathrm{RSS}^2) < 0 at the stationary point. Evaluating at 𝜷=𝜷̂\boldsymbol\beta = \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} gives the joint MLE σ̂MLE2=RSS(𝜷̂)/n\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}} = \mathrm{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})/n.

p_full = X.shape[1]           # 6 = intercept + 5 predictors

sigma2_mle      = rss / n
sigma2_unbiased = rss / (n - p_full)

print(f"RSS at beta_hat                        = {rss:.6f}")
print(f"sigma^2 MLE      = RSS / n     = RSS/{n}  = {sigma2_mle:.6f}   (sd = {np.sqrt(sigma2_mle):.6f})")
print(f"sigma^2 unbiased = RSS / (n-p) = RSS/{n - p_full}   = {sigma2_unbiased:.6f}   (sd = {np.sqrt(sigma2_unbiased):.6f})")
print(f"true sigma^2                           = {sigma_true**2:.6f}   (sd = {sigma_true:.6f})")
print(f"\nratio unbiased / MLE = {sigma2_unbiased / sigma2_mle:.6f}   vs   n/(n-p) = {n/(n - p_full):.6f}")
RSS at beta_hat                        = 41.775504
sigma^2 MLE      = RSS / n     = RSS/100  = 0.417755   (sd = 0.646340)
sigma^2 unbiased = RSS / (n-p) = RSS/94   = 0.444420   (sd = 0.666649)
true sigma^2                           = 0.490000   (sd = 0.700000)

ratio unbiased / MLE = 1.063830   vs   n/(n-p) = 1.063830

Why the denominators differ. Both estimates use the same numerator, RSS(𝜷̂)\mathrm{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}); they differ only in whether the divisor is nn or n−p−1=94n - p - 1 = 94. The residual vector is not the error vector: it is 𝒓=(𝑰−𝑯)𝜺\mathbf r = (\mathbf I - \mathbf H)\boldsymbol\varepsilon, the projection of 𝜺\boldsymbol\varepsilon onto the (n−p−1)(n - p - 1)-dimensional space orthogonal to the columns of 𝑿\mathbf X. Fitting six coefficients uses up six dimensions’ worth of the noise, so E[RSS]=(n−p−1)σ2=94σ2E[\mathrm{RSS}] = (n - p - 1)\sigma^2 = 94\sigma^2, not nσ2n\sigma^2. Dividing by nn therefore gives E[σ̂MLE2]=94100σ2<σ2E[\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}] = \frac{94}{100}\sigma^2 < \sigma^2: the MLE is biased downward, systematically understating the noise by 6% here. Dividing by the residual degrees of freedom n−p−1n-p-1 corrects exactly for this. Numerically, 0.41780.4178 versus 0.44440.4444 — the unbiased estimate is nearer the true σ2=0.49\sigma^2 = 0.49. Maximum likelihood is not required to be unbiased, and here it is not; the two agree asymptotically since n/(n−p−1)→1n/(n-p-1) \to 1.

(c) Profile of ℓ\ell along the 𝒙2\mathbf x_2 coordinate

With 𝒆x2=(0,0,1,0,0,0)𝖳\mathbf e_{x_2} = (0,0,1,0,0,0)^{\mathsf T}, plot ℓ(𝜷̂+t𝒆x2,σ̂MLE2)\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} + t\,\mathbf e_{x_2}, \widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{MLE}}) for t∈[−1.25,1.25]t \in [-1.25, 1.25].

def loglik(b, s2):
    resid = y - X @ b
    return -n / 2 * np.log(2 * np.pi * s2) - (resid @ resid) / (2 * s2)

e_x2 = np.zeros(p_full)
e_x2[2] = 1.0                       # index 2 = the x2 column (0 = intercept)

t_grid = np.linspace(-1.25, 1.25, 501)
ll_grid = np.array([loglik(beta_hat + t * e_x2, sigma2_mle) for t in t_grid])

t_star = t_grid[np.argmax(ll_grid)]
print(f"grid maximizer     t* = {t_star:.6f}")
print(f"log-likelihood at t*  = {ll_grid.max():.6f}")
print(f"log-likelihood at t=0 = {loglik(beta_hat, sigma2_mle):.6f}")
print(f"beta_hat[x2] = {beta_hat[2]:.6f}  ->  beta_hat[x2] + t* = {beta_hat[2] + t_star:.6f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.plot(t_grid, ll_grid, color="#1f77b4", lw=2)
ax.axvline(0.0, color="#d62728", ls="--", lw=1.2, label="$t = 0$ (least-squares fit)")
ax.plot([t_star], [ll_grid.max()], "o", color="#d62728", ms=7, label=f"maximum at $t = {t_star:.3f}$")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\ell(\hat\beta + t\,e_{x_2},\ \hat\sigma^2_{MLE})$")
ax.set_title("Profile log-likelihood along the $x_2$ coordinate")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.show()
grid maximizer     t* = 0.000000
log-likelihood at t*  = -98.250851
log-likelihood at t=0 = -98.250851
beta_hat[x2] = -0.841489  ->  beta_hat[x2] + t* = -0.841489

Where the maximum occurs and why. The curve peaks at t=0t = 0, that is, exactly at 𝜷̂\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} itself, with ℓ=−98.251\ell = -98.251. This agrees with the least-squares result for the reason established in part (a): with σ2\sigma^2 held fixed, ℓ\ell is a strictly decreasing affine function of RSS\mathrm{RSS}, and RSS\mathrm{RSS} is minimized over all of ℝ6\mathbb R^6 at 𝜷̂\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}. A line through the global minimizer must attain its minimum RSS — hence its maximum ℓ\ell — at the point where it passes through that minimizer, namely t=0t = 0.

The shape is also informative. Expanding, RSS(𝜷̂+t𝒆)=RSS(𝜷̂)+t2𝒆𝖳𝑿𝖳𝑿𝒆\mathrm{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta} + t\,\mathbf e) = \mathrm{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}) + t^2\,\mathbf e^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X\mathbf e; the cross term −2t𝒆𝖳𝑿𝖳𝒓-2t\,\mathbf e^{\mathsf T}\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf r vanishes by the orthogonality established in Question 1(c). So the profile is an exact downward parabola centered at t=0t=0, with curvature −‖𝒙2‖2/σ2-\lVert \mathbf x_2 \rVert^2 / \sigma^2. The sharpness of that parabola is the observed information for βx2\beta_{x_2}: a steep peak means the data pin the coefficient down tightly, a flat one means they do not — a point that returns forcefully in Question 4.

Question 3 (Starting values in nonconvex optimization)

f(x)=exp⁡(1.5x)−3(x+6)2−0.05x3,f′(x)=1.5exp⁡(1.5x)−6(x+6)−0.15x2.f(x) = \exp(1.5x) - 3(x+6)^2 - 0.05x^3, \qquad f'(x) = 1.5\exp(1.5x) - 6(x+6) - 0.15x^2.

(a) Plot ff over [−40,7][-40, 7]

def f(x):
    return np.exp(1.5 * x) - 3 * (x + 6)**2 - 0.05 * x**3

def fprime(x):
    return 1.5 * np.exp(1.5 * x) - 6 * (x + 6) - 0.15 * x**2

xs = np.linspace(-40, 7, 4000)
fs = f(xs)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))

axes[0].plot(xs, fs, color="#1f77b4", lw=1.8)
axes[0].set_ylim(-600, 600)
axes[0].set_title("$f(x)$ on $[-40, 7]$  (y-axis clipped)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[0].set_ylabel("$f(x)$")
axes[0].axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.6)
axes[0].grid(alpha=0.3)

zoom = (xs >= -12) & (xs <= 7)
axes[1].plot(xs[zoom], fs[zoom], color="#ff7f0e", lw=1.8)
axes[1].set_title("zoom on $[-12, 7]$: the exponential wall")
axes[1].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[1].set_ylabel("$f(x)$")
axes[1].axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.6)
axes[1].grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# locate the stationary points on a fine grid for reference
sign_change = np.where(np.diff(np.sign(fprime(xs))) != 0)[0]
print("approximate stationary points (grid):", np.round(xs[sign_change], 3))
print(f"f(-40) = {f(-40):.3f},   f(7) = {f(7):.3f}")
approximate stationary points (grid): [-32.654  -7.362   2.346]
f(-40) = -268.000,   f(7) = 35791.353

Features that matter for optimization.

  1. The function is nonconvex and has multiple stationary points. On the plotted interval there are three: a local minimum near x≈−32.6x \approx -32.6, a local maximum near x≈−7.4x \approx -7.4, and a second local minimum near x≈2.35x \approx 2.35. Any gradient-based method converges to whichever basin its starting point lies in, so the answer depends on x(0)x^{(0)}.
  2. Two separate basins of attraction, split by the local maximum at x≈−7.4x \approx -7.4. Roughly, starts to the left of −7.4-7.4 descend to the left minimum; starts to the right descend to the right minimum.
  3. Wildly different scales across the domain. For x≲−10x \lesssim -10 the exponential term is numerically negligible and ff behaves like a cubic of magnitude in the hundreds; near x=7x = 7, exp⁡(1.5x)≈3.6×104\exp(1.5x) \approx 3.6\times10^4 and the function rises almost vertically. The curvature f″f'' therefore changes by orders of magnitude, which makes a single fixed step size hopeless and makes line searches essential — BFGS’s own curvature estimate must adapt as it moves.
  4. Overflow risk on the right. A line search that overshoots to, say, x=500x = 500 would evaluate exp⁡(750)\exp(750) and return inf. The exponential wall punishes aggressive steps taken from the right-hand basin.
  5. The two local minima have very different objective values (−390.4-390.4 versus −175.9-175.9), so landing in the wrong basin is not a harmless difference — it costs more than 200 units of objective.

(b) BFGS from x(0)=−15x^{(0)} = -15 and x(0)=0x^{(0)} = 0

def run_bfgs(x0):
    res = minimize(
        fun=lambda v: f(v[0]),
        x0=np.array([float(x0)]),
        jac=lambda v: np.array([fprime(v[0])]),
        method="BFGS",
    )
    x_end = res.x[0]
    return {
        "start": float(x0),
        "final_x": x_end,
        "f_final": f(x_end),
        "abs_grad": abs(fprime(x_end)),
        "converged": bool(res.success),
        "message": res.message,
        "iterations": res.nit,
        "f_evals": res.nfev,
    }

results = [run_bfgs(-15), run_bfgs(0)]

for res in results:
    print(f"start x0 = {res['start']:>6.1f}  ->  x = {res['final_x']:>12.6f}   "
          f"f(x) = {res['f_final']:>12.6f}   |f'(x)| = {res['abs_grad']:.3e}   "
          f"converged = {res['converged']}")
    print(f"{'':>17}({res['message']}; {res['iterations']} iterations, {res['f_evals']} function evaluations)")

runs = pd.DataFrame(results).rename(columns={
    "start": "start x0", "final_x": "final x", "f_final": "f(x)", "abs_grad": "|f'(x)|",
    "f_evals": "f evals",
})

start x(0)x^{(0)} final xx f(x)f(x) |f′(x)|\lvert f'(x)\rvert converged
−15-15 −32.649111-32.649111 −390.385770-390.385770 2.8×10−142.8\times10^{-14} yes
00 2.3499672.349967 −175.862620-175.862620 8.1×10−68.1\times10^{-6} yes

Both runs report successful convergence, and in both cases the gradient at the returned point is numerically zero, so each is a legitimate stationary point — indeed a local minimum, since f″>0f'' > 0 at both.

(c) Why the runs differ

Why different answers. BFGS is a local descent method. It is guaranteed only to find a point where the gradient vanishes, and which one it finds is determined entirely by which basin of attraction contains x(0)x^{(0)}. The local maximum at x≈−7.4x \approx -7.4 separates the domain into two basins. Starting at x(0)=−15x^{(0)} = -15 puts the optimizer to the left of that ridge, where f′>0f' > 0, so descent moves left and settles in the left minimum at x=−32.649x = -32.649. Starting at x(0)=0x^{(0)} = 0 puts it to the right, where the local gradient sends it right, into the minimum at x=2.350x = 2.350. Neither run can see over the ridge: the algorithm only ever uses local function and gradient information, and there is no mechanism in BFGS to escape a basin once it is in one. Both answers are “correct” as solutions to the first-order condition; they are answers to a local question, not a global one.

Which is lower. The run from x(0)=−15x^{(0)} = -15, at f(−32.649)=−390.386f(-32.649) = -390.386, is lower by 214.5214.5 than the run from x(0)=0x^{(0)} = 0, at f(2.350)=−175.863f(2.350) = -175.863.

What more would be needed to claim a global minimum. A converged optimizer plus a zero gradient establishes only local optimality. To argue globally one would want:

  • Many starting values. A multi-start over a grid or random draws covering the region of interest, checking that no start produces a lower value; or a global method (simulated annealing, basin hopping, DIRECT).
  • A dense grid or bracketing evaluation of ff over the domain to confirm no lower region was missed — and, since ff is smooth, enumeration of all roots of f′f' with a classification of each by the sign of f″f''.
  • Control of the behavior outside the plotted window. The interval [−40,7][-40, 7] is a plotting choice, not part of the problem. As x→+∞x \to +\infty, exp⁡(1.5x)\exp(1.5x) dominates and f→+∞f \to +\infty; as x→−∞x \to -\infty, −0.05x3→+∞-0.05x^3 \to +\infty and again f→+∞f \to +\infty. So ff is coercive, only finitely many stationary points exist, and the global minimum over ℝ\mathbb R is attained — it is the smaller of the two local minima, f(−32.649)=−390.386f(-32.649) = -390.386. Without an argument of this kind (or a proof of convexity, which fails here), one can only report the best point found.

Question 4 (Nearly collinear predictors)

Set seed 43202, draw ui∼iidN(0,1)u_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1), and define

𝒙6=𝒙1+10−4𝒖,𝑿+=[𝑿𝒙6],𝒚⋆=𝒚+10−3𝒖.\mathbf x_6 = \mathbf x_1 + 10^{-4}\mathbf u, \qquad \mathbf X_+ = [\mathbf X \ \ \mathbf x_6], \qquad \mathbf y^\star = \mathbf y + 10^{-3}\mathbf u.

(a) Fit 𝒚\mathbf y on 𝑿\mathbf X and on 𝑿+\mathbf X_+

x6 = x1 + 1e-4 * u

y_star = y + 1e-3 * u

The explanation. Since 𝒚⋆−𝒚=10−3𝒖\mathbf y^\star - \mathbf y = 10^{-3}\mathbf u and 𝒙6−𝒙1=10−4𝒖\mathbf x_6 - \mathbf x_1 = 10^{-4}\mathbf u,

𝒚⋆−𝒚=10(𝒙6−𝒙1),\mathbf y^\star - \mathbf y = 10\,(\mathbf x_6 - \mathbf x_1),

verified above to machine precision. The perturbation therefore lies exactly inside the column space of 𝑿+\mathbf X_+. Least squares is linear in the response, so the fit of 𝒚⋆\mathbf y^\star is the fit of 𝒚\mathbf y plus the fit of the perturbation; and because the perturbation is already in the column space, it is reproduced exactly, with coefficient vector −10-10 on 𝒙1\mathbf x_1 and +10+10 on 𝒙6\mathbf x_6 and zero elsewhere. Hence

𝜷̂⋆=𝜷̂++10(𝒆x6−𝒆x1),𝒚̂⋆=𝒚̂+10(𝒙6−𝒙1)=𝒚̂+10−3𝒖,\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}^\star = \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_+ + 10(\mathbf e_{x_6} - \mathbf e_{x_1}), \qquad \widehat{\mathbf y}^\star = \widehat{\mathbf y} + 10(\mathbf x_6 - \mathbf x_1) = \widehat{\mathbf y} + 10^{-3}\mathbf u,

which is exactly what the numbers show: changes of ∓10.000000\mp 10.000000 in the coefficients, and a shift in fitted values whose root mean square is ‖10−3𝒖‖/n≈10−3\lVert 10^{-3}\mathbf u\rVert / \sqrt n \approx 10^{-3}.

The asymmetry is entirely a matter of scale. The direction 𝒙6−𝒙1\mathbf x_6 - \mathbf x_1 has norm ≈10−3\approx 10^{-3} while 𝒙1\mathbf x_1 has norm ≈10\approx 10: it is a near-null direction of 𝑿+\mathbf X_+, the one associated with the tiny smallest singular value that produces the condition number of 2×1042\times10^4. Moving along it changes the prediction almost not at all, so an enormous coefficient movement is needed to accomplish the tiny required change in 𝒚̂\widehat{\mathbf y}. In the language of Question 2(c), the log-likelihood surface has an almost perfectly flat ridge in the (β1,β6)(\beta_1, \beta_6) plane along the direction β1+β6=const\beta_1 + \beta_6 = \text{const}; the location along that ridge is pinned down only by the negligible part of the data, so noise slides the solution far along it while the fit is unaffected.

What this suggests about interpreting nearly collinear predictors. Separate effects should not be interpreted. What the data determine well here is the sum β1+β6\beta_1 + \beta_6 — an estimable, stable, low-variance quantity that did not change at all under the perturbation — and the fitted values, which are similarly stable. The individual coefficients are not determined by the data in any practical sense: they have huge standard errors, unstable and implausible signs and magnitudes (−1330-1330 and +1331+1331 when the true effect is 1.41.4), and they respond violently to changes in the response too small to notice. Reporting “𝒙1\mathbf x_1 has a large negative effect and 𝒙6\mathbf x_6 a large positive one” would be an artifact of the near-degeneracy, not a finding. A good training RMSE is no defense — prediction was essentially unaffected throughout. The practical responses are to drop one of the redundant predictors, combine them, or use a penalized method such as ridge regression that stabilizes the near-null direction; and to always inspect the condition number before reading individual coefficients.

Question 6 (Can 39 million Fitbit records represent US adults?)

Setting. Patten et al. (2026) describe Fitbit data on 59,018 All of Us participants over 14 years, comprising more than 39 million daily step records. Participants entered by one of two routes: BYOD, sharing data from a Fitbit they already owned, and WEAR, receiving a Fitbit at no cost after being invited. In the general activity cohort the two groups had 32,035 and 22,474 participants. Comparing BYOD to WEAR: 77.3% versus 55.1% reported being White; 6.1% versus 15.2% reported household income between $10,000 and $25,000; and median daily steps were 6,867 versus 5,797.

Target of estimation. The mean of participant-specific average daily step counts among US adults during the study period, with each adult weighted equally.

The claim under evaluation. “This dataset contains more than 39 million daily Fitbit records. Therefore, the average of all recorded step counts should provide an accurate estimate of mean daily activity among US adults.”

(a) Are the 39 million daily records independent observations?

No. The 39 million records come from only 59,018 people — an average of roughly 660 days each. Days contributed by the same person are strongly positively correlated: a habitual runner produces a long series of high-step days and a sedentary office worker a long series of low-step days, so records cluster tightly within individuals. The effective sample size is governed much more by the 59,018 participants than by the 39 million rows. Records within a person are also serially dependent over time (weekday/weekend cycles, seasons, injuries, life events). Treating the rows as 39 million independent draws would understate standard errors by a large factor, producing a spuriously precise answer — precision about the wrong quantity is not a virtue.

What makes some participants contribute more recorded days than others. The number of days a person contributes is itself an outcome, driven by characteristics plausibly related to activity:

  • Adherence and wear-time habits. People who enjoy tracking, and who consistently charge and wear the device, log more days. Enthusiasm for step tracking is correlated with walking more.
  • Fitness motivation and goal-setting. Someone using the device to train for an event wears it daily; someone who bought it out of curiosity may abandon it in a drawer within weeks.
  • Length of enrollment and device ownership. BYOD participants can retrospectively share years of pre-existing data, whereas WEAR participants start accumulating only after receiving the device. This alone creates a systematic difference in days per person between the two groups.
  • Device continuity and resources. Replacing a broken or outdated Fitbit, and maintaining smartphone and internet service to sync, requires money and technical comfort — both associated with socioeconomic status, which is itself associated with activity patterns.
  • Health and life circumstances. Illness, hospitalization, disability, caregiving demands, or shift work interrupt wear; sustained good health supports long uninterrupted series. Attrition is not random.
  • Age and technology comfort, which affect both sustained device use and typical step counts.

How averaging all recorded days weights participants unequally. A simple average over the 39 million rows is

y‾rows=∑i∑t=1diyit∑idi=∑iwiy‾i,wi=di∑jdj,\bar{y}_{\text{rows}} = \frac{\sum_{i} \sum_{t=1}^{d_i} y_{it}}{\sum_i d_i} = \sum_i w_i \,\bar y_i, \qquad w_i = \frac{d_i}{\sum_j d_j},

a weighted average of participant means y‾i\bar y_i with weights proportional to each person’s number of recorded days did_i. A participant with 3,000 recorded days counts 100 times as much as one with 30. The stated target instead gives every adult weight 1/N1/N. So even setting sampling aside, the row average estimates the wrong functional whenever did_i is associated with y‾i\bar y_i — precisely what the mechanisms above imply, with the highly adherent, motivated, higher-step users dominating the sum. A person-level average (compute each participant’s mean, then average those, or weight rows by 1/di1/d_i) matches the target’s weighting; the naive row average does not.

(b) Does the BYOD–WEAR step difference show that owning a Fitbit causes people to walk more?

No. The comparison is observational, and participants were not randomized to the two routes — they selected into BYOD by already owning a Fitbit, and into WEAR by being invited and accepting a free device. The groups differ markedly on measured characteristics before any step is counted: 77.3% versus 55.1% White, and 6.1% versus 15.2% in the $10,000–$25,000 income band, meaning WEAR participants are substantially more likely to be from lower-income households and from racial and ethnic groups under-represented in BYOD. Where groups differ this visibly on the variables we can see, they almost certainly differ on the ones we cannot. The 1,070-step gap in medians therefore confounds any device effect with everything else that distinguishes the two populations.

Plausible alternative explanations.

  1. Self-selection on pre-existing activity (the main one). Buying a Fitbit with one’s own money is something already-active people do — runners, walkers, gym-goers, people already invested in fitness. WEAR participants were recruited by invitation, including many who would never have purchased a tracker and who had no particular fitness motivation. The higher BYOD median most likely reflects who chooses to buy a step tracker, i.e. reverse causation: walking more causes Fitbit ownership rather than the other way around.
  2. Socioeconomic confounding. Income differs sharply between the groups, and income is associated with walkable neighborhoods, safe places to exercise, leisure time, occupation type, and health status — all direct determinants of daily steps. Race and ethnicity likewise track structural differences in neighborhood walkability and access. These confound the group comparison entirely.
  3. Differential measurement and wear patterns. Experienced BYOD owners have established habits of wearing the device during walks and workouts, while a new WEAR user may wear it inconsistently, forget it on active days, or remove it during work — producing lower recorded steps without any difference in actual steps. Retrospective BYOD data may also be filtered toward the periods when the person was engaged with the device.

A causal claim would need randomization of device provision (as in a trial) or, failing that, careful adjustment for measured confounders with an explicit argument about unmeasured ones — and even then the pre-existing-activity difference would be very hard to rule out.

(c) How selection can bias an estimate even in a very large dataset

Sample size reduces variance, not bias. Bias is a property of who enters the data, and it does not shrink as nn grows: with a selected sampling process, a larger dataset converges more and more precisely to the wrong number. This is the “big data paradox” — a huge but selected sample can be less trustworthy than a small probability sample, because tight confidence intervals around a biased center create false confidence.

Selection of participants (who is in the data). Getting into this dataset requires clearing several filters, none of them random. A person must (i) know about and volunteer for All of Us — volunteers are not a random draw of US adults; (ii) either already own a Fitbit, which requires disposable income, technological comfort, and interest in fitness tracking, or be invited to WEAR and accept; and (iii) own a compatible smartphone with data service and consent to share their data continuously. Each filter is associated with step counts. The visible evidence of this is in the numbers given: BYOD is 77.3% White versus 55.1% for WEAR, and only 6.1% of BYOD report income of $10,000–$25,000 versus 15.2% of WEAR. Neither group matches the US adult distribution, and the 59,018 participants overall over-represent people who are healthier, wealthier, more health-conscious, more digitally connected, and more research-engaged than US adults generally. People without smartphones, without stable housing or internet, with severe disability, in institutional settings, or simply uninterested in fitness tracking are largely absent — and their step counts are systematically different from those of the people who are present.

Selection of recorded days (which days are in the data). Conditional on being a participant, days enter the data only if the device was worn, charged, and synced. This is again non-random and plausibly related to the outcome itself: people are more likely to wear a tracker on days they intend to be active, and more likely to leave it off when sick, injured, traveling, hospitalized, or having an unusually sedentary day. Missing days are thus not missing at random but concentrated among low-step days, so even a within-person mean over recorded days can overstate that person’s true average. As shown in (a), the number of recorded days also varies enormously across people in a way tied to adherence and motivation.

Why the naive average of all recorded daily step counts fails. It misses the target on three compounding counts:

  1. Wrong population. It averages over All of Us Fitbit users, not US adults. The dataset is not a probability sample, so no sampling weights link it to the US adult population and nothing about the 39 million records makes the participants representative.
  2. Wrong weighting. Even within the observed participants, it weights each person by did_i rather than equally, so the most adherent and device-engaged people — a group whose activity differs systematically from the rest — dominate the estimate. This alone means it does not estimate the stated target.
  3. Wrong days. Within a person, recorded days over-represent worn days, and wear is associated with activity, so even the person-level means being averaged are themselves biased upward relative to true average daily steps.

None of these problems is repaired by having more rows; adding records from the same selected participants makes the estimate more precisely wrong. (The direction of the net bias is not the question here, and is genuinely uncertain without external information — the selection mechanisms do not all point the same way, and are plausibly upward on health-consciousness but confounded by device-wear patterns and the mix of BYOD and WEAR.)

What would help. Post-stratification or raking to known US adult demographic totals; person-level rather than row-level averaging; explicit wear-time criteria (for instance, restricting to days with a minimum wear duration and to participants with a minimum number of valid days) with sensitivity analyses; modeling the missing-day mechanism; and, most convincingly, benchmarking against a probability sample with objective accelerometer measurement such as NHANES. The dataset is genuinely valuable — its scale supports within-person and subgroup analyses that no small survey can — but for estimating a population mean, representativeness, not volume, is what matters.
